opening.headline: Learn how agents created by different teams collaborate through A2A and how to distinguish between their roles and MCP.
body: As the number of agents increases, you will need to exchange work with agents created by other teams or partners. Collaboration is difficult if you have to know the other person’s insides every time. You need a common commitment to ask for work and receive results without showing your true intentions.

In this class, we will look at the life cycle of A2A's three roles and five communication elements, the Agent Card that introduces the other party, and the Task that handles lengthy tasks. Next, we will check the horizontal and vertical distinction with MCP, and how to use A2A in ADK and when not to use it through scenarios.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of A2A, Agent Card, and Task life cycle
You can distinguish MCP and A2A depending on the connection target and decide where to use A2A and where not to use it.
Can explain why webhook notifications need to be verified and that the Agent Card is a self-declaring document

screens.title: How do I talk to an agent created by another team?
screens.lead: First, read the situation where three teams each created an agent. Read while thinking about what we need to know to communicate with each other.

visual.alt: A scene where three agents written in different languages cannot communicate and only exchange question marks.
labels: How many hours does it take?

paragraphs: Our team's order agent was written in Python. The inventory agent was created in Java by another team, and the shipping agent was created by the partner using their own framework. The three agents operate in different languages ​​and tools, and the ordering agent must ask “Is this product in stock?”

If you can only ask questions if you know the other person's internal code or tools, collaboration will soon be blocked. Moreover, partners do not want to disclose their internal memory or tool implementation. What you need is a common commitment to ask for work and receive results without showing your true intentions.

Time is also an issue. If the inventory check takes several hours, should you keep the connection open or receive a notification when it's finished? How should the conversation continue if the other person asks, “Which warehouse should we use as a reference?”

There is only one question in this class. What should be the common promise used by agents who do not know each other? One of these promises is the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, and it also covers how it differs from the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting tools and data to agents.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Can I connect the same way between calling up a tool like a calculator or a weather query and leaving the work to an agent from another team who makes a decision and asks back?

screens.outro: Let me first think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever had the experience of meeting individual specifications each time while linking with another team or an external company's system?
items.answer: If the specifications are different for each partner, you have to adjust them every time you connect, and if the partner changes, you have to start over from the beginning. The same is true between agents, so having common protocols significantly reduces connection costs. A2A, which is covered in this class, is one of those common protocols.

items.prompt: Have you ever worried about waiting for a result because the response from the other system takes a long time?
items.answer: You can keep the connection open and wait, ask periodically, or tell it to notify you when it's done. Which one is right depends on how long the operation will take and whether the connection may be lost. A2A supports all three methods.

items.prompt: How did connecting tools feel different than entrusting the work to a person or other agent?
items.answer: Tools like calculators give you input and produce a certain output. When you entrust a task to someone, you ask questions, it takes time, and the situation changes in the middle. This difference is the standard that divides MCP and A2A, and the key is whether the other party is a tool or an agent.

We look at the roles and components of A2A, the Agent Card that introduces the other party, and the life cycle of the Task that handles lengthy tasks. Next, we will explain the horizontal and vertical distinction between MCP and how A2A is used in ADK, as well as when it should not be used.

screens.outro: First, let's look at the three roles and five communication elements of A2A.

screens.title: A2A Key Concepts: Three Roles and Five Elements
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term to see an explanation. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: A2A (Agent2Agent) is an open standard that enables communication and collaboration between agents in applications built by different frameworks and providers, with internal workings remaining hidden. Three roles emerge in the interaction: the user, who defines a goal or is an automated service; A2A Client, which is an app, service, or other agent that initiates communication on behalf of the user; and A2A server, which is a remote agent that processes requests via the selected protocol binding. The remote agent is referred to as black box for the client. Internal operations, memory, and tools remain hidden. The fundamental elements of communication consist of five components: an Agent Card, which is a document introducing an agent; a Task, which is a work unit with a state; Message, which represents a turn in a conversation; Part, which is a unit that contains content; and Artifact, which is the output generated by a task. A2A v1.0 supports JSON-RPC, gRPC, and HTTP+JSON bindings. The JSON-RPC binding uses JSON-RPC 2.0 messages over HTTP(S). Part contains exactly one of text, binary file, file URL, or structured JSON, enabling any content format to be transmitted.

terms.tip: An app, service, or other agent that initiates communication on behalf of a user. This is the one sending the request.
It is a remote agent that opens an HTTP endpoint that implements the protocol, receives requests, processes tasks, and returns results or status.

It is an invisible system. The client has no knowledge of the remote agent's internal memory and tool implementation, and collaborates only based on its declared capabilities and what is communicated.
It is a one-turn conversation between the client and the agent. It contains roles (user or agent) and content and delivers instructions, questions, answers, and status notifications.
It is the unit that contains the actual content within the message and output. Contains exactly one of the following: text, binary file, file URL, or structured JSON.
The actual artifacts, such as documents, images, and structured data, created by agents during their work. It may be delivered in small portions.
This is the message format used in A2A's JSON-RPC binding. Transmission takes place over HTTP(S).

screens.outro: Among these, let's look at the Agent Card, which introduces the agent, in more detail.

screens.title: Agent Card: Agent's digital business card
screens.lead: When you select a highlighted passage in the description below, an explanation will appear explaining what the Agent Card does.

data.text: An Agent Card is a JSON metadata document describing an agent's identity, capabilities, endpoints, skills, and authentication requirements. A client reads the card to assess suitability for the task, construct requests, and establish secure communication. Finding cards to learn which A2A servers exist and what they can do is called discovery. Cards may be found at a well-known address, `https://{server domain}/.well-known/agent-card.json`, in a catalog of agents, or at a preconfigured address. Authentication requirements are declared in the card. Credentials are usually sent through HTTP headers, separated from protocol messages. After authentication, a more detailed extended card may be available. Cards can be digitally signed: Verifying the signature confirms that the card has not been tampered with and is from the provider it claims to be.. However, a card is a self-declared document, so a signature does not guarantee that its claimed capabilities are accurate. Messages and artifacts from remote agents also become model inputs: treat them as untrusted input and do not blindly follow embedded instructions. A card lets collaboration begin based on declared capabilities without knowing the other agent's internals.

marks.span: identity, capabilities, endpoints, skills, and authentication requirements
marks.note: These are five pieces of information included on the card. Write down in one place who you are, what you can do, where the request is being sent, what skills you offer, and what certifications are required.
The client's first purpose is to read the card. Even if you don't know the opponent's insides, you can judge whether it's worth entrusting this agent with the abilities declared on the card.
This is the process where the client finds the Agent Card to find out which A2A servers exist and what they can do. Collaboration begins with discovery.
This method places the card in a designated path under the domain. Alternatively, you can search through a catalog of agents or set a card address in advance.

Authentication requests are declared on the card and credentials (OAuth tokens, API keys, etc.) are sent as HTTP headers. This means that the secret value will not be mixed with the conversation content.

marks.span: Verifying the signature confirms that the card has not been tampered with and is from the provider it claims to be.
marks.note: Card signatures follow the JSON Web Signature (JWS, RFC 7515) format and are optional. The signature is a means of verifying the authenticity and integrity of the card.

The card is a self-introduction. Even if there is a signature, it does not guarantee that the abilities stated there are actually the same, so if it is your first time collaborating with someone, you must separately decide whether to trust them.

The remote agent's response goes into my model's input. If the model follows the instructions hidden therein, it becomes prompt injection, so minimum privileges and approval are applied in the same manner as the tool results.
This is the principle of collaborating with opaque agents. Even without showing any internal memory or tools, you can get started as long as you have an open contract called a card.

screens.outro: Once you've found your partner with a card, let's look at tasks that take a long time to complete.

screens.title: Task life cycle and interaction method
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and follow step by step whether the agent's response is a Message or a Task and what state the Task goes through.

steps.title: Response is Message or Task
steps.body: If the agent can respond immediately, it responds with a Message. If the task takes a long time, a new Task is returned. A Task is a stateful unit of work with a unique ID and a defined life cycle, so clients can track its progress by that ID.

steps.title: In progress status
steps.body: The main statuses are SUBMITTED and WORKING. The enumerated values ​​of the specification are prefixed, such as TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED, and are called without the prefix in this class. Reception and processing are separated, so clients can see whether the request has reached the other party and whether work has actually begun.

steps.title: halt state
steps.body: INPUT_REQUIRED is a stopped state because additional user input is required, and AUTH_REQUIRED is a stopped state because authentication is required. The specification distinguishes between these two as halt states. Since both are not finished, the same Task will continue if you give the required value. However, the mere fact that it is changed to AUTH_REQUIRED does not mean that a specific operation is permitted, and the scope and confirmation method of permission are determined by the agent implementation.

steps.title: exit status
steps.body: Exit statuses are COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELED, and REJECTED. REJECTED is when the agent decides not to take action. If you send a message to a terminated task, an error will occur indicating that the task is not supported, so subsequent requests will proceed to a new task. At this time, contextId connects the context by grouping related tasks.

steps.title: Three ways to receive results
steps.body: Request/response and polling are methods in which the client periodically asks for the status and checks if it takes a long time. SSE streaming is where a server continuously streams progress over an HTTP connection opened by a client. Push notifications allow the server to call a webhook on the client when an important update is available, making them ideal for very long tasks or disconnected clients. A webhook is a method in which a server sends an HTTP request to an address known in advance by the client. The specification states that the server sends the set authentication information in the request, and the client verifies whether the notification is real using the authentication information and checks whether the Task ID in the notification is the one it created. Since the same notifications may come repeatedly, they must be processed idempotently, and the server must reject webhook addresses pointing to the internal network to prevent attacks (SSRF) that trick the server into calling an internal address.

steps.title: The output is Artifact
steps.body: The result of the work is delivered as an Artifact, not a Message. Artifacts are actual artifacts with a unique ID and name, and may be streamed in chunks as the work progresses.

screens.title: A2A and MCP: horizontal and vertical
screens.lead: Select the "MCP" and "A2A" buttons alternately to compare the different connection directions and destinations of the two protocols.

visual.alt: A diagram showing A2A, which connects agents horizontally, and MCP, which connects agents and tools vertically.

states.label: MCP (vertical)
states.body: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard that allows agent apps to become clients and connect to servers that serve up tools and data, and servers provide tools, resources, and prompts. MCP makes one agent deep. Adding an MCP connection gives that agent one more tool, resource, or skill. Opponents are simple primitives with defined inputs and outputs. Examples include calculators, database queries, and weather APIs. In the garage example, the MCP involves the mechanic agent using a diagnostic scanner or repair manual database. In summary, MCP gives depth to agents.

states.label: A2A (horizontal)
states.body: A2A goes beyond agent boundaries and reaches agents from other teams, departments, and partners. Your opponent is an autonomous system that reasons, plans, uses multiple tools, and converses over multiple turns. Discover each other, negotiate, and exchange information. In the garage example, the conversation between the customer and the manager agent is A2A. In summary, A2A gives your system reach. The two protocols are not substitutes but are used together. Agents collaborate with each other through A2A, and each agent uses its own tool as MCP.

screens.outro: Now let's take a look at how ADK handles A2A.

ext.title: Model Context Protocol, What is MCP?
Model Context Protocol Specification, Server features

screens.title: ADK's A2A integration and agent gateway
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how ADK supports A2A in both directions, its distinction from local subagents, and the role of the gateway.

tabs.label: side exposed
tabs.body: To make my agent visible to other places in Google's agent framework, Agent Development Kit (ADK), I use the A2AServer component. This component makes the agent code accessible over the network, so clients from other teams can send requests to this agent using A2A protocols.

tabs.label: side to use
tabs.body: The side that uses the remote A2A agent uses RemoteA2aAgent. Because this client handles network communication, authentication, and data formatting, it feels similar to writing a local tool or function for the developer. The fact that it's remote isn't very obvious in the code.

tabs.label: Separate from local subagent
tabs.body: Subagents within the same process communicate quickly in memory and are used to organize code. If it is a separate service, operated by a different team, created in a different language, or requires strict contracts, use A2A. The two methods differ depending on where the communication boundary is located.

tabs.label: When not to use it
tabs.body: Local subagents are better when you need to separate modules within a single agent, have performance-critical internal operations, or share memory or context directly. If you use A2A in these places, network call and serialization costs will only increase and you will gain nothing. ADK's A2A integration also supports preserving inference traces, tracking long-running tool calls, and delivering file output.

tabs.label: gateway
tabs.body: As the number of agents increases, a gateway that handles authentication, routing, and access policies in one place is used. A2A is easy to combine with these middle layers because it declares its authentication needs on the Agent Card. The advantage is that there is no need to enter a separate security code for each agent.

screens.title: Explanation 1: MCP connects tools, A2A connects agents
screens.lead: The instructor walks through a scenario and identifies whether each call is MCP or A2A. Read the table from top to bottom.

data.caption: Classification by call in “order is late” inquiry
rows: Customer tells support agent, “My order is late”
The support agent will be the entity handling this inquiry.
Support agent queries his order database
The support agent gives the tool
My agent directly calls the basic elements with determined input and output.
Ask the partner delivery agent to inform you of the location of this case and the reason for the delay.
Partners communicate while hiding their internal tools. The other party is the judging agent.
Delivery agent checks its own tracking system
It is the use of internal tools that are not visible to the calling party.
data.notes: As a result, it is divided into A2A between agents and MCP between agents and tools. The criteria for distinction is not technology, but what the opponent is. If the input and output are fixed, it is a tool, and if it reasons and asks questions and takes several turns, it is an agent. Going back to the garage example, a conversation between a customer and a manager agent coordinating a repair schedule would be A2A, while a mechanic agent reading a diagnostic scanner or looking up a repair manual database would be MCP. Even if two protocols overlap within a system, you can tell them apart by looking at whether each call is directed to a tool or an agent. This distinction applies anew for each call.

screens.outro: This time, we will solve long-consuming delegation tasks into Tasks.

screens.title: Explanation 2: Solving long-consuming delegation tasks into tasks
screens.lead: Move the slider to request “global inventory count results” from your partner inventory agent and follow the process over time. The explanation changes for each step.

stops.body: Since this is a request that can take several hours, the response is not a Message but a new Task. The client will receive a Task ID and will know that the submission has been confirmed as SUBMITTED. From now on, we will track your progress with this ID. What the client has at this point is not the result, but the promise of receiving the result later.

The status is WORKING. The method of checking progress is chosen according to the situation. If the delay is short, check periodically through polling, if you want to watch in real time, use SSE streaming, and if the connection may be lost, you will be notified of completion through push notification.

If the other party asks “Which warehouse should this be based on?” the Task stops at INPUT_REQUIRED. Since it is not a failure but an interruption, the same task continues when the client gives an answer.

When the work is finished, it becomes COMPLETED and the result comes as an Artifact. No further messages can be sent to a terminated Task, but subsequent requests can continue the previous context by using the same contextId. To summarize, long-running delegation does not end with a single Message, but is tracked by Task ID and stops and resumes when necessary, ending with an Artifact. The client does not need to keep the connection open; it only needs to check its status.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's decide where to use A2A and where not to use it.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Where to use A2A and where not to use it
screens.lead: Select and expand each situation to see whether A2A or a local subagent is right for you and why.

items.title: An external financial data company provides quotes as an A2A agent.
items.body: A2A is correct. Since it is a separate service and operated by a different organization, you must read the Agent Card and make a request using standard protocols without knowing the inside. You don't need to know your opponent's implementation, just check the abilities and authentication requirements declared on the card.

items.title: Ordering, inventory, and delivery services are independent microservices.
items.body: A2A is correct. Because communication crosses network boundaries, a standard contract is required, and long-running tasks for each service can be handled as tasks. Even if the team for each service is different, the same protocols are used, so there is no need to redefine the connection method when adding a new service.

items.title: The core logic is Python, but the legacy part is Java.
items.body: A2A is correct. Even if the languages ​​are different, if you use a standard communication layer, both sides can collaborate without having to know each other's implementation. Start collaborating without rewriting your legacy.

items.title: DataValidator to cleanse input within an agent
items.body: A local subagent is appropriate. The purpose is to organize code and memory communication is fast. Dividing into networks only increases costs.

items.title: Subtasks that need to share context directly with the main agent
items.body: A local subagent is appropriate. Context needs to be shared directly, but separating it over a network actually gets in the way. The criterion for judgment is the communication boundary. If the boundary lies within a process, it is called local; if it crosses a service or organization, it is called A2A.

screens.title: Concept map revisited
screens.lead: The following flashcards summarize the main concepts of this lesson. Select a card to flip it over, and select the right arrow to go to the next card.

cards.back: There are three roles: user, client agent, and remote agent, and they communicate through Agent Card, Task, Message, Part, and Artifact. Remote agents are black boxes. Parts contain text, files, or structured data and allow for the exchange of content in any format.

An agent's business card declaring capabilities, endpoints, skills, and certification requirements. Clients discover their opponents by card and determine if they are up to the task. Authentication requests are declared on the card and credentials are sent separately as HTTP headers.

You can go from SUBMITTED to WORKING, stop with INPUT_REQUIRED or AUTH_REQUIRED, and end with COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELED, or REJECTED. No further messages can be sent to a completed Task, and the context of subsequent requests is continued using contextId.
A2A is a horizontal connection between agents, and MCP is a vertical connection between agents and tools. They are used together rather than replaced.

I expose my agent as A2AServer and write a remote agent as RemoteA2aAgent. The gateway can handle authentication, routing, and access policies in one place. Division of labor within the same process is faster with local subagents.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the judgment criteria at once.

screens.title: Key points and judgment checklist
screens.lead: Read the summary below and think about the final reflection question for yourself. There are no items to submit or grade.

paragraphs: A2A is an open standard that allows hidden agents to collaborate under common protocols. The client discovers the opponent with the Agent Card, tracks progress with a Message if the answer comes immediately, or a Task if it takes a long time, and receives the result as an Artifact. This theorem can be rewritten as three questions:

When choosing a connection, you just need to ask three questions in that order: First, is the other party a tool with fixed input and output, or an agent that makes judgments and asks questions? If it's a tool, it's MCP, if it's an agent, it's A2A. Second, does the other party need to be in the same process and share memory or context directly? Then a local subagent is better. Third, does the work take a long time or can you ask questions in the middle? If so, choose the appropriate method among Task status and polling, streaming, or push notification. After asking this question, the connection method is usually determined.

A2A is used when crossing service, organization, and language boundaries, and division of labor within the same process is done with local subagents. As the number of agents increases, a configuration that has a gateway in charge of authentication, routing, and access policies can be used. Lastly, remember that the distinction between MCP as a tool and A2A as an agent is not based on the name of the technology, but rather on the nature of the opponent. Even within the same system, the distinction can vary from call to call.

checks.q: What is the appropriate thing for a client to do when receiving A2A push notifications (webhooks)?

Verify whether the notification is real with the set authentication information, and check whether the Task ID in the notification is the task you created.

glossary.def: It is an open protocol that allows invisible agents to communicate and collaborate.
This is a JSON business card that describes the agent's identity, capabilities, endpoints, skills, and authentication requirements.
A stateful unit of work with a unique ID and life cycle.
Deliverables such as documents, images, and data created by agents during work.
This is a client that allows ADK to use a remote A2A agent like a local tool.
The server sends an HTTP request to an address previously known by the client, and the recipient must verify the sender.

misconceptions.fact: The two take different directions and write together. MCP connects agents and tools, and A2A connects agents and agents.

misconceptions.myth: To use A2A, you need to know the opponent's internal tools and memory.
misconceptions.fact: The opponent is unclear. Collaborate only with declared capabilities and exchanged information.

misconceptions.myth: All sub-agents must connect via A2A.
misconceptions.fact: Division of labor within the same process is faster and simpler with local subagents.

misconceptions.myth: If it is written on the Agent Card, the ability is guaranteed.
misconceptions.fact: The card is a document in which the agent declares himself. Although the signature can confirm whether it has been tampered with and the issuer, it is not a guarantee that the ability is real, and the other party's response must also be treated as untrusted input.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: A2A is an open standard that allows hidden agents to collaborate under common protocols.
The Agent Card becomes the starting point for discovery and connection by declaring capabilities, endpoints, and authentication requirements.
A Task is a stateful unit of work that goes through a suspension state and a termination state and delivers the results to an Artifact.
MCP is a vertical connection between agents and tools, and A2A is a horizontal connection between agents.
Division of labor within the same process is done with local subagents, and A2A is used when crossing service, organization, and language boundaries.
